title: Given an image as a grid of pixel colors, a starting pixel, and a new color, repaint the starting pixel and all connected pixels of the same original color with the new color, where connectivity is orthogonal. Return the modified image.
shortTitle: Flood Fill: BFS/DFS from starting cell

s1_definition.oneliner: From the starting cell, DFS or BFS recoloring every connected cell of the original color to the new color, guarding against the no-op case where new equals old.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Flood fill** – a traversal from a starting cell that recolors every orthogonally connected cell sharing the starting cell's original color to a new color.
- **No-op guard** – if the new color equals the original color, return immediately to avoid infinite recursion or reprocessing.
- **Visited marker** – when new and old colors differ, the new color itself acts as the visited marker because a recolored cell no longer matches the original.
- **DFS approach** – recursively recolor the current cell and its four neighbours.
- **BFS approach** – use a queue to spread the recoloring level by level, preferred for large connected regions to avoid stack overflow.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a risk heat map lets an analyst click a contiguous block of same-status cells and reclassify them to a new status. Flood fill spreads the new status across the connected region and stops at cells of a different status. The equal-status guard makes reclassifying to the same value a safe no-op rather than an infinite loop.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flood Fill recolors a connected region of a grid starting from a given cell, repainting every orthogonally connected cell that shares the starting cell's original color. The solution records the original color, runs a DFS or BFS from the start, and recolors each matching cell while spreading to its four neighbours.

The single most important detail is the no-op guard: if the new color equals the original color, return immediately. Without this guard, a recolored cell still matches the original condition, so the traversal would revisit it indefinitely, causing infinite recursion. With distinct colors, a recolored cell no longer matches the original, so the new color itself acts as the visited marker.

The time and space are both proportional to the size of the connected region. For very large regions, BFS is preferred to avoid deep recursion. The problem is essentially the island traversal but seeded from one arbitrary cell instead of sweeping the whole grid.

At the National Bank of India, the risk heat map lets analysts reclassify a contiguous block of same-risk cells by clicking one cell. Flood fill spreads the new risk level across the connected region, and the no-op guard ensures that reclassifying to the same level is a safe no-op. This pattern is the same one behind paint bucket tools and region selection in image editors.

Remember one sentence: from the start cell, DFS or BFS recolors all connected same-color cells, and the no-op guard when new equals old prevents infinite recursion.

---

keyPoints: Record the starting cell's original color and run DFS or BFS to recolor every connected cell of that color.
The no-op guard is essential: if new color equals original, return immediately to prevent infinite recursion.
When new and old colors differ, the new color acts as the visited marker so no separate visited matrix is needed.
Time and space are both O(region size) where the region is the connected component of the starting cell.
BFS is preferred for large regions to avoid stack overflow from deep recursion.
This is the same traversal pattern as Number of Islands but seeded from a single specified cell.
